awd_titl_txt: Travel: 2025 International Workshop on Verification of Scientific Software (VSS)
awd_abstract_narration:
This award provides student travel support for the 2025 International Workshop on Verification of Scientific Software (VSS) to be held as a satellite workshop of ETAPS 2025 (International Joint Conferences on Theory and Practice of Software), on Sunday, May 4, 2025, at McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario, Canada.    

The VSS workshop provides an important and valuable educational opportunity for students to study foundational topics that lie at the intersection of scientific computing and verification. The significance and importance of the workshop arises because scientific software plays an increasingly important role in scientific and engineering disciplines: Weather prediction, drug discovery, the design of buildings, vehicles, and aircraft, simulations of astrophysical phenomena, and prediction of seismic activity are some of the many applications. In these contexts, verification itself must overcome new challenges posed by resilience, floating-point computations, and massive parallelism. The significance and importance of the workshop include disseminating novel ideas for implementing and reasoning about reliable scientific software; building international community and cooperation in foundational research areas; and enhancing education of US students, including underrepresented groups, by exposure to and interaction with leading-edge research and researchers. By supporting US-based students, the school will thus train the next generation of researchers and practitioners in both industry and academia.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The Verified Software Systems (VSS) 2025 Workshop, held in conjunction with the ETAPS conference in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada at the McMaster University Campus brought together leading researchers, practitioners, and students working at the intersection of formal methods, high-performance computing (HPC), machine learning (ML), and scientific software reliability. The workshop’s primary objective was to facilitate technical presentations, discussions, community building, and cross-disciplinary exchange on methods for verifying, analyzing, and improving the correctness of complex scientific software systems—an increasingly essential challenge as HPC and ML applications scale to extreme levels of computational performance.


A major impact of this NSF-supported activity was the funding of travel for eight students from across the United States. These students represented a broad geographic and institutional distribution. The travel support enabled these students to attend the workshop in person, engage with its technical content, and interact directly with luminaries in formal verification, HPC correctness, compiler technologies, and scalable scientific computing.


The students served as session scribes, helping document technical presentations and Q&A exchanges. This scribing responsibility provided invaluable exposure to the students. It exposed them to the broader culture of scientific research.


By lowering financial barriers to the students and providing direct access to leading researchers, this project strengthened the pipeline of future scientists and engineers in HPC, ML, and software verification. Building a workforce proficient in trustworthy, scalable scientific software is vital for the nation’s competitiveness in computational science, engineering, and national security. The VSS 2025 workshop contributed meaningfully to this long-term goal by fostering early-career engagement and broadening of awareness in advanced scientific computing research.
